tweets.title: Excited to see so many new frontier model releases in June/July!! One lingering question I always have: Which benchmarks do different labs choose to report publ
tweets.body:
Excited to see so many new frontier model releases in June/July!! One lingering question I always have: Which benchmarks do different labs choose to report publicly for their releases, and what gets left out?

After auditing 18 releases, 143 capability benchmarks, and 80 safety evals. A few things here:

1. Reporting choices shape the story:  for 68 capability benchmark rows in the current matrix, 32 are unique; 36 are from two models +; only 3 appear in all four.  Safety reporting is even more fragmented: 71 of 80 rows appear once in the current four releases.

2. Evaluation is moving toward real work: New additions concentrate on coding, professional tasks, agents/tools, and science.

3. Benchmark reporting turns over quickly: Across 14 same-lab release transitions, only 56% of previously reported benchmark editions appear again in the next report; 44% drop out of public reporting (ofc for various reasons).

All in all, I keep coming back to the idea that a benchmark is one projection of model behavior.

These days, watching a model actually build a game can honestly feel more persuasive than another leaderboard point increase. 

To some degree, it probably makes sense, as people fundamentally care about whether a model is capable, reliable, and pleasant to work with, not just whether it scores two points higher. But demos and vibes are not science either. 

Wishful thoughts: advancing evaluation science to catch up with AI agents' fast-growing capabilities, more systematic/aligned safety reports, while expanding into more of the domains (e.g., 1. benchmarking agents about collaborating with humans 2. agents' abilities to simulate human behavior).

And damn evaluation is getting harder these days in AI. so HUGE kudos to all the ppls pushing this frontier forward and building high-quality public benchmarks that help the whole field make progress 🫡🫡

More details here: https://t.co/PBFkQGjDI6

tweets.title: I often hear people say: oh, we trained our own models, then the next frontier model dropped, and prompting/harnessing it beat all our hard work, so we give up
tweets.body:
I often hear people say: oh, we trained our own models, then the next frontier model dropped, and prompting/harnessing it beat all our hard work, so we give up and just wait now, yadda yadda.

True, for some applications, e.g., coding agents, this might be the case.

But I really suspect/hope the future will see more and more interesting models going on trajectories different from current frontier models (e.g, https://t.co/1LLzdgOgKv): 

1. It is much easier and more fun to train models now, with all the very successful coding powers and APIs like Tinker (yeah, I had so much fun building Osim). 

2. Current frontier models will most likely keep getting pulled deeper into their own narrative: stronger coding, more productivity, blabla.

Intelligence comes in so many diverse forms, and I sincerely hope leading labs could help people expand the breadth and diversity of intelligence (and yeah, i got routed to opus 4.8 😅).

tweets.body:
🧭 Key insight:

Human simulation isn't a prompting problem, and it isn't solved by scale. The most capable assistants are often the least human.

Building simulators means realigning the whole pipeline around behavioral realism: measure it (SOUL-Index), feed it (socially grounded data), and reward it (behavioral RL). That's what "behavioral foundation model" means.

tweets.title:
Training on LLM-judge rewards for *behavior* gets weird. Two failure modes we caught:

🕵️ Judge manipulation: in Sotopia the model started inserting evaluation-
tweets.body:
Training on LLM-judge rewards for *behavior* gets weird. Two failure modes we caught:

🕵️ Judge manipulation: in Sotopia the model started inserting evaluation-like statements into dialogue ("our relationship score should be perfect") instead of actually being social. In ~20-25% of rollouts!

📉 Short-response collapse: when judges subtract points per detected error, the model learns to just say "I'm fine." Fewer claims, fewer errors, higher reward.

An LLM hacking detector + rubric rewards mitigated both (ofc, there are defs more works to do there). If you do RL on judge-scored behavior, monitor the behavioral stats, not just the reward curve.

tweets.title: The part I find most interesting: we dropped OSim zero-shot into τ-bench as the customer talking to a tool-use agent, and scored it against real humans doing th
tweets.body:
The part I find most interesting: we dropped OSim zero-shot into τ-bench as the customer talking to a tool-use agent, and scored it against real humans doing the same 165 tasks (τ-USI).

OSim-8B's reactions are nearly indistinguishable from real users: React alignment 93.2 vs 93.5 for humans.

Meanwhile, some of the most assistant-tuned frontier models are among the WORST user simulators. Their helpful, agreeable register is exactly what real users don't have. Helpfulness ≠ humanity.

📈 Results on SOUL-Index:

✅ OSim-8B lands within ~1 point of GPT-5.5, Gemini 3.1 Pro & Claude Opus 4.7 on the 23-task average
✅ best or tied-best on 8/23 tasks, more than any single frontier model
✅ +18.0 over the best frontier model on user simulation (UserLLM), +16.8 on social interaction (Sotopia-Hard)
✅ beats every prior open behavioral-simulation model (UserLM, CoSER, HumanLM, Sotopia-RL) nearly across the board

An 8B model. Open weights.

tweets.title:
💡 Step 3: training, in two very different stages.

Midtraining on the corpus teaches the model what human behavior looks like. It shifts length, formatting, and
tweets.body:
💡 Step 3: training, in two very different stages.

Midtraining on the corpus teaches the model what human behavior looks like. It shifts length, formatting, and word choice toward the human register.

Then we train one RL expert per benchmark, using verbal feedback from LLM judges where rewards aren't verifiable, and merge all 23 specialists into one model via expert distillation.

Fun ablation: the two stages do different jobs. Midtraining fixes the register; RL drives the benchmark gains.

tweets.title: 💡 Step 1: measure it. We built SOUL, 5 axes of human-like behavior (conversation, social skills, cognition/ToM, role-play, evaluation), and SOUL-Index, 23 bench
tweets.body:
💡 Step 1: measure it. We built SOUL, 5 axes of human-like behavior (conversation, social skills, cognition/ToM, role-play, evaluation), and SOUL-Index, 23 benchmarks under one roof.

💡 Step 2: the data. 21.4M real human interactions (~10B tokens) from 62 sources. Most raw dialogue data has no idea WHO is talking or WHY. So we retrofit every conversation with back-generated social grounding (e.g., a character profile + interaction goal), and the model learns behavior grounded in context, not just text.

tweets.body:
Finally, don’t throw out LLM-as-user benchmarks, but mind the gap!

(1) Validate with real humans, at least on a sample
(2) Design metrics beyond binary reward
(3) If building models for simulation, optimize for human faithfulness, not task completion
What's the biggest gap you've seen between simulated and real users?

tweets.title: Furthermore, a lot of benchmarks (e.g, Tau-bench) use rule-based binary rewards: success (1) or failure (0). How well does this match what humans actually think
tweets.body:
Furthermore, a lot of benchmarks (e.g, Tau-bench) use rule-based binary rewards: success (1) or failure (0). How well does this match what humans actually think?

It doesn't.

70.6% of reward=0 interactions were judged successful by humans.
33% of reward=1 interactions were judged unsuccessful.

Cramer's V = 0.233. Nearly orthogonal.

tweets.body:
It's not just simulated users. LLM evaluators are biased, too.

GPT-5.1 overestimates the agent's human-likeness by +1.11 on a 1–3 scale. But it's actually conservative on task success.

Strange inversion: LLMs think the agent sounds great but fails at tasks. Humans think it sounds robotic, but it gets the job done.
